A useful next question is how the same monthly $100 plan would have looked with a different historical window or contribution cadence, rather than treating this run as a forecast.

From September 10, 2025 through September 9, 2026, this test was a story of a small cloud company becoming closely associated with the artificial intelligence boom. DigitalOcean reported that third-quarter 2025 revenue rose 16 percent to $230 million, annual recurring revenue reached $919 million, and demand was strong enough that it was adding data-center and graphics-chip capacity. Management also said it expected its growth targets to arrive earlier than previously planned. [DigitalOcean's third-quarter results](https://investors.digitalocean.com/news/news-details/2025/DigitalOcean-Announces-Third-Quarter-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx) support the business-growth part of that explanation.

The optimism continued into the next report. For the fourth quarter, DigitalOcean reported revenue of $242 million, up 18 percent from a year earlier, and said its 2025 revenue reached $901 million. It also raised its outlook for 2026 and highlighted growing demand from AI customers. [The company's full-year results](https://investors.digitalocean.com/news/news-details/2026/DigitalOcean-Announces-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Financial-Results/) are evidence that the business was improving. It is reasonable to infer that investors rewarded the shares for the combination of faster growth, larger customers, and AI demand, although those reports cannot explain every daily price move.

By August 2026, the acceleration was more visible. DigitalOcean reported second-quarter revenue of $281.2 million, up about 29 percent year over year, and earnings above the analyst estimate. The shares initially fell after the report before recovering, which shows what holding DOCN was like: good company news could still produce sharp swings because investors were judging the results against very high expectations. [Reporting on the second-quarter results](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/digitalocean-q2-2026-slides-ai-growth-drives-29-revenue-surge-93CH-4834748) documents that immediate reversal.

The test began with $1,000 and added $100 each month. Across 13 fills, it put $2,300 into DOCN and ended at $6,644.07. That equals a 188.87 percent return on the contributions. The path was not smooth: the portfolio's worst fall from an earlier high was -42.12 percent, and its highest recorded value was $8,648.60. In practical terms, someone holding through the period had to watch a large portion of the gains disappear at one point, without knowing whether the decline would stop. The regular purchases helped spread the entry prices across the year, but they did not remove the risk of a large fall in a single volatile stock. The test also includes small trading costs of 10 basis points in fees and 5 basis points in slippage per trade.

SPY, the benchmark representing a broad basket of large US companies, returned 12.07 percent over the same window. DOCN therefore beat it by 176.8 percentage points. The comparison says more about concentration than about a typical stock experience: one company tied to a powerful AI and cloud theme rose far more than the broad market, but it also exposed the holder to a much deeper setback. The result was excellent for this particular historical period, while the large drawdown shows the price paid for that concentration.

SPY had a generally positive year, but the ride was uneven. The market benefited early in the period from hopes for lower interest rates and continued enthusiasm around large technology and chip companies. Reuters reported that the Federal Reserve cut rates in September 2025, after which the S&P 500 reached a record high, helped by chip stocks and expectations of further cuts. That is evidence for a strong start to the period, although it does not by itself prove why this particular strategy entered or exited.

The test then went through a meaningful setback. The strategy's value rose to 1038.57 USD before its largest decline, then fell to 988.47 USD by the bottom. In everyday terms, the account temporarily dropped below its original 1000.0 USD, and that decline lasted from December 5, 2025 to March 30, 2026. The measured drop from the previous high was -4.82 percent. For someone holding through it, this would have felt like several months of watching an earlier gain disappear before the account recovered.

The broader market also reached new highs in January 2026. Reuters attributed one record close to Broadcom and other chipmakers, alongside expectations that the Federal Reserve might cut rates. The later weakness had a different feel. Reporting from Reuters and Nasdaq described a March selloff driven by the widening Iran conflict, sharply higher oil prices, renewed inflation worries, higher interest rates, and a broad reduction in investors' willingness to take risk. These reports are evidence about the market backdrop. It is an inference, not a direct measurement from the backtest, that these events helped produce the difficult stretch seen in the strategy's results.

By the end of the test, the portfolio had recovered and finished at its highest recorded value, 1085.97 USD. The test therefore made money overall, but it captured only part of SPY's gain. Its total return was 8.6 percent, compared with 16.89 percent for the benchmark. Because the benchmark was SPY itself, this was not a comparison between different assets. It was a comparison between holding SPY through the period and using the RSI threshold rules to change exposure to that same asset. The rules lagged the simple benchmark by 8.29 percentage points.

There were 4 executed fills. The available results do not establish how many complete buy-and-sell trades occurred, so it would be misleading to describe the exact trading decisions. The most reasonable reading is that the RSI rules changed the portfolio's exposure only a few times, and those changes reduced participation in some of SPY's gains, especially during the strong parts of the period. The strategy still ended higher, but holding SPY continuously would have produced the better result over this tested window.

SPY had a generally positive year, but the ride was uneven. The market benefited early in the period from hopes for lower interest rates and continued enthusiasm around large technology and chip companies. Reuters reported that the Federal Reserve cut rates in September 2025, after which the S&P 500 reached a record high, helped by chip stocks and expectations of further cuts. That is evidence for a strong start to the period, although it does not by itself prove why this particular strategy entered or exited.

The test then went through a meaningful setback. The strategy's value rose to 1038.57 USD before its largest decline, then fell to 988.47 USD by the bottom. In everyday terms, the account temporarily dropped below its original 1000.0 USD, and that decline lasted from December 5, 2025 to March 30, 2026. The measured drop from the previous high was -4.82 percent. For someone holding through it, this would have felt like several months of watching an earlier gain disappear before the account recovered.

The broader market also reached new highs in January 2026. Reuters attributed one record close to Broadcom and other chipmakers, alongside expectations that the Federal Reserve might cut rates. The later weakness had a different feel. Reporting from Reuters and Nasdaq described a March selloff driven by the widening Iran conflict, sharply higher oil prices, renewed inflation worries, higher interest rates, and a broad reduction in investors' willingness to take risk. These reports are evidence about the market backdrop. It is an inference, not a direct measurement from the backtest, that these events helped produce the difficult stretch seen in the strategy's results.

By the end of the test, the portfolio had recovered and finished at its highest recorded value, 1085.97 USD. The test therefore made money overall, but it captured only part of SPY's gain. Its total return was 8.6 percent, compared with 16.89 percent for the benchmark. Because the benchmark was SPY itself, this was not a comparison between different assets. It was a comparison between holding SPY through the period and using the RSI threshold rules to change exposure to that same asset. The rules lagged the simple benchmark by 8.29 percentage points.

There were 4 executed fills. The available results do not establish how many complete buy-and-sell trades occurred, so it would be misleading to describe the exact trading decisions. The most reasonable reading is that the RSI rules changed the portfolio's exposure only a few times, and those changes reduced participation in some of SPY's gains, especially during the strong parts of the period. The strategy still ended higher, but holding SPY continuously would have produced the better result over this tested window.
